podcast.title: Beatles' Release Strategy (1963-1965)
podcast.body: During 1963-1965, The Beatles employed a prolific release strategy, putting out up to a dozen singles per year, which were then consolidated into two annual albums, a model cited as a precedent for the constant flow of new music required from artists today. "Artists need to deliver a constant flow of new songs, just like the Beatles did through the year 1963, 64 and 65, when they'd release up to a dozen singles and then summarize them with two albums a year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canada's Early Embrace (1963-1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles were embraced in Canada nearly a year before their breakthrough in the United States, with songs like "All My Love," "Roll Over Bay, Tovon," and "Twist and Shout" exclusively available there. Capitol Records Canada played a crucial role by manufacturing these records north of the 49th parallel and then exporting at least 100,000, and potentially up to 350,000, copies of each song to the US. "Although the United States gets a lot of attention because it's where the Beatles made their TV debut, it was in Canada where they were embraced first."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Christmas Flexi-Discs (1963-1969)
podcast.body: The Beatles were notable for their extensive use of flexi-discs, sending out special Christmas flexi-discs to their fan club every year between 1963 and 1969. "The Beatles loved these things. Between 1963 and 1969, they sent out special Christmas flexis to the fan club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disastrous Merchandising Deal (1963)
podcast.body: In 1963, Beatles manager Brian Epstein licensed the band's merchandising rights to Nikki Bern's company, Selltab (Beatles spelled backwards). This deal secured only 10% of revenues for The Beatles and is estimated to have cost the band over $100 million over the years, despite selling a wide array of items from wigs to bubblegum. "In retrospect, this was a stupid deal, securing just 10% in revenues for the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Canadian Disinterest (1963)
podcast.body: Despite their eventual global success, The Beatles initially struggled to gain traction in Canada in early 1963. Capitol Records Canada reported very low sales for their early singles: "Love Me Do" sold 170 copies, "Please Please Me" sold 280, and "From Me to You" sold 300, suggesting Canada was initially uninterested. "It seemed that Canada was not interested in the Beatles, but that all changed with the release of She Loves You in September 1963."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Encounter at Heathrow (1963)
podcast.body: In late 1963, renowned American TV host Ed Sullivan was delayed at Heathrow Airport in London. While waiting for his flight back to the States, he observed a large commotion caused by young girls excitedly gathering around four young men. Intrigued, Sullivan made inquiries about the group and was reportedly impressed by what he learned.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Initial Publishing Control by Northern Songs (February 1963)
podcast.body: In February 1963, The Beatles' music publishing was managed by Northern Songs, a company owned by Dick James, their manager Brian Epstein, John Lennon, and Paul McCartney. "In the beginning, this would be February 1963, the publishing for the Beatles music was handled by a company called Northern Songs. The owners were Dick James, Manager Brian Epstein, John Lennon, and Paul McCarty."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Royal Variety Performance (1963)
podcast.body: In late 1963, before their departure for the United States, The Beatles famously concluded their set with "Twist and Shout" during their performance at Queen Elizabeth's Royal Variety. "the group famously closed their set with it at Queen Elizabeth's Royal Variety performance."

podcast.title: 1964 Cultural Impact
podcast.body: Starting in 1964, The Beatles' arrival marked a period in the 1960s where every day brought something new, exciting, and groundbreaking to music, profoundly shaping the decade's history. "starting with the Beatles in 1964 every day seemed to bring something new, something exciting and something groundbreaking."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: 1964 North American Tour & Ed Sullivan Appearance
podcast.body: By the spring of 1964, The Beatles had achieved massive popularity not only in their home country but also across North America. This included performances in New York, Washington, and Miami in February, alongside their famous appearance on the Ed Sullivan Show, all generating immense buzz. "In February, the group had played New York, Washington and Miami, had appeared on the Ed Sullivan show, and they were attracting the same sort of buzz they had at home."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: American Beatlemania Peak (1964)
podcast.body: The period around 1964, marked by the success of "I Want to Hold Your Hand" and subsequent number ones, represented the dizzying peak of American Beatlemania. "It was the dizzying peak of American Beatlemania."

podcast.title: Around the Beatles (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles starred in a TV special produced by Jack Good, titled "Around the Beatles," where Millie Small also made an appearance. "appearing on Around the Beatles, a special starring the Beatles and produced by Jack Good."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Beatlemania in America (1964)
podcast.body: "Can't Buy Me Love" was released in March 1964 at the height of the first wave of Beatlemania in America, demonstrating the intense public anticipation and demand for their music during this period. The song's rapid ascent to number one, despite not debuting there, underscored their cultural dominance. "Released in March of 1964 at the height of the first wave of Beedle Mania in America."

podcast.title: Brief Montreal Stay (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles played two concerts at the Montreal Forum on September 8, 1964, performing a 12-song set for 9,500 fans at 5:20 pm and another show for 11,500 fans at 8:30 pm. They chose not to stay in Montreal, instead flying directly to Jacksonville, Florida, having been in the city for only eight hours. "The band stayed in Montreal for only 8 hours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brief Vancouver Performance (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' concert in Vancouver on August 22, 1964, despite the massive anticipation and crowd frenzy, lasted only 27 minutes. They played 11 songs, notably omitting "I Want to Hold Your Hand," one of their biggest hits at the time. Immediately after the show, the band was whisked away to Vancouver International Airport and flown straight to Los Angeles, marking their one and only performance in Western Canada. "Then just 27 minutes after they arrived on stage, they left."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bryce Decker's Airport Escapade (1964)
podcast.body: On August 18, 1964, local high school student Bryce Decker took a daring chance at Winnipeg airport during The Beatles' refueling stop. He ran across the runway, climbed the plane's stairs, and nearly entered the aircraft before being restrained by security, an escapade that was captured in a series of photographs. Decker later recalled seeing the band members chuckling as security wrestled with him, having "just did it for a bit of fun" without realizing its significance. "After arriving at the airport, he ran across the runway, up the stairs, and nearly got into the plane before he was grouted by security."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chaotic Toronto Airport Arrival (1964)
podcast.body: On September 6, 1964, over 10,000 young people stormed Toronto's international airport to catch their first glimpse of The Beatles. The frenzied crowd jostled behind a 60-meter chain-link fence, belting out verses from their chart-topping tracks and screaming in a way the city had never heard before. "Behind a 60 meter chain link fence, the frenzy crowd jostled for position and belted out verses from chart crushing tracks such as, Please, please me, love, be, do, and she loves you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Concert Logistics at Maple Leaf Gardens (1964)
podcast.body: For the September 6, 1964, concerts at Maple Leaf Gardens, a detailed plan was devised to get The Beatles safely to the venue. Limousines served as a decoy, drawing fans while the band slipped out the back door of the King Edward Hotel and into a paddy wagon, which smuggled them into the Gardens. A five-block area around the venue was sectioned off 12 hours prior, transforming downtown Toronto into "Beedleland." "Limos were to pull up at the King Edward Hotel, as expected, as fans pounded at the vehicles like zombies the band would dug out the back door and into a patty wagon that would smuggle them into the gardens."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cultural Storm Example (1964-1970)
podcast.body: The Beatles are cited as a prime example of a "perfect cultural storm" in music, where musical, social, political, and demographic conditions converged, with their most impactful era spanning from 1964 to 1970. "Think of the Beatles from 64 to 70."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cultural Storm Example (1964-1970)
podcast.body: The Beatles' influence from 1964 to 1970 was cited as an example of a "perfect cultural storm" in music, similar to punk rock, grunge, and Britpop. "Think of the Beatles from 64 to 70."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decca Records Rejection (Pre-1964)
podcast.body: The band was famously rejected by at least one record label, Decca, whose executives felt that "guitar groups were on the way out" and that "The Beatles have no future in show business." "A band famously rejected by at least one record label, Deca, because they felt that guitar groups were on the way out."

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Debut - February 1964
podcast.body: The Beatles' appearance on Ed Sullivan in February 1964 inspired countless people to form bands, significantly changing music across all genres within just seven years. Despite their breakup in 1970, they are still regarded as the most influential rock group of all time. "how many stories have you heard about people deciding to form a band after seeing the Beatles on Ants Sullivan in February 1964?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Performance - John Cummings' Inspiration (1964)
podcast.body: John Cummings (later Johnny Ramone) was deeply influenced by seeing The Beatles perform on The Ed Sullivan Show in 1964, sparking his love for the guitar. "He had been in love with the guitar ever since he saw the Beatles' plan Ed Sullivan back in 1964."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
podcast.body: Their legendary appearance on the Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, marked the beginning of rock's second cycle. This event "rescued Rock" and created a "tsunami that spread across the planet," influencing music for the remainder of the 1960s. "Cycle 2 starts 13 years later with the American TV debut The Beatles on the Ed Sullivan Show, February 9th, 1964."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
podcast.body: In 1964, The Beatles appeared on the Ed Sullivan show, presenting a fresh new sound that significantly helped America emerge from the national funk following the assassination of JFK. This event is considered by some to be the true beginning of the 1960s in terms of rock music. "In 1964, the Beatles appeared on the Ed Sullivan show with a fresh new sound that helped drag America out of the funk that followed the assassination of JFK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' appearance on Ed Sullivan in February 1964 inspired countless people to form bands, significantly changing music across all genres within just seven years. Despite their breakup in 1970, they are still regarded as the most influential rock group of all time. "how many stories have you heard about people deciding to form a band after seeing the Beatles on Ants Sullivan in February 1964?"

podcast.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' debut performance on The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, is considered a watershed moment that irrevocably changed rock and roll forever. This pivotal event, which profoundly reshaped music history, might not have happened had Sullivan's flight not been delayed and if The Beatles had not coincidentally been at Heathrow Airport at the same time.

podcast.title: Extreme Conditions at Toronto Concert (1964)
podcast.body: The atmosphere inside Maple Leaf Gardens on September 6, 1964, was intensely hot and muggy, with temperatures around 30 degrees Celsius outside and even higher inside. Soda and ice cream vendors ran out of supplies, and water fountains barely functioned, yet the fervent fans' dehydration and exhaustion were no match for their enthusiasm. "It was a hot, muggy, late summer day with temperatures at around 30 degrees Celsius. Inside the venue it was even hotter, and soda and ice cream vendors were running out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First North American Tour Stop in Winnipeg (1964)
podcast.body: On a warm, cloudy day in mid-August 1964, The Beatles were flying from London to San Francisco for their inaugural major North American tour, making an unplanned refueling stop in Winnipeg. This stop unexpectedly turned into a major event when CJAYTV's Bob Burns announced their arrival on local radio, leading to the airport being swarmed by frenzied fans. "The band landed on August 18, 1964 at 2.5pm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Official Canadian Performance in Vancouver (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' first official Canadian concert and performance took place on August 22, 1964, at the Pacific National Exhibition (PNE) in Vancouver, British Columbia. The PNE is an annual 15-day summer fair and amusement park. "And the concert was held at the Pacific National Exhibition in Vancouver, British Columbia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Friendship with The Ronettes (1964)
podcast.body: During The Ronettes' brief UK tour in early 1964, they became friendly with The Beatles. Ronnie had a "brief chaste flirtation" with John Lennon, and Estelle had a "little more" with George Harrison. "they became friendly with the Beatles, Ronnie had a brief chaste flirtation with John Lennon, and Estelle something a little more with George Harrison."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 110: "Be My Baby" by the Ronettes

podcast.title: Hotel Invasion by Fans (1964)
podcast.body: During The Beatles' stay at the King Edward Hotel in Toronto in September 1964, teens relentlessly bypassed security, creating an "infestation" for which the hotel seemed to have "no repellent." At 3 am, radio journalist Larry Cain, traveling with the band, encountered a teen in an oversized housekeeping uniform knocking on his door, asking for soap and then if he could take her to The Beatles. "Teens kept getting past security. It was as if the hotel was dealing with an infestation for which they had no repellent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Identical Second Toronto Concert (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' second concert at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto, which began at 10 pm on September 6, 1964, was virtually identical to the first. It featured screaming fans, blinding flash bulbs, raining lipsticks and bras, resulting in continued frenzy and fainting among the audience, echoing the "mass hysteria" of the earlier show. "If you've seen footage from a Beatles concert, you can imagine that the second concert was identical to the first."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' debut performance on The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, is considered a watershed moment that irrevocably changed rock and roll forever. This pivotal event, which profoundly reshaped music history, might not have happened had Sullivan's flight not been delayed and if The Beatles had not coincidentally been at Heathrow Airport at the same time.

podcast.title: Impact on Guitar Band Demand (1964)
podcast.body: Following The Beatles' arrival in America in February 1964, there was an unprecedented surge in demand for electric guitars, as countless aspiring musicians were inspired to form guitar bands. This event marked a significant turning point in the popularity of the electric guitar. "After the Beatles hit America in February 1964, everyone wanted to be in a guitar band. Demand for new instruments exploded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

podcast.title: John Lennon's Clash with Red Robinson (1964)
podcast.body: Halfway through the Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, as the crowd neared rioting, local radio host Red Robinson was instructed to go on stage to calm the fans. John Lennon, unaware of the situation, confronted Robinson, telling him, "Get off our stage, nobody interrupts the Beatles," before relenting after Robinson explained that manager Brian Epstein had sent him. "John looked down at Brian Epstein, the band's manager who gave him the okay. John turned Robinson and said, Okay, carry on mate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: King Edward Hotel Frenzy (1964)
podcast.body: Upon their arrival at the King Edward Hotel in downtown Toronto on September 6, 1964, a frenzy of fans greeted The Beatles, leading to Paul McCartney having his shirt torn and Ringo Starr being separated from John and George. Although police quickly restored order on the street, Beatlemania continued inside, where a 14-year-old girl was found hiding in the linen closet of their royal suite. "Paul would have a shirt torn open by a fan, wrangle with separated from John and George, but thankfully police were able to quickly restore order on the street and get the band into the hotel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mass Hysteria at Maple Leaf Gardens (1964)
podcast.body: Upon The Beatles' appearance on stage at Maple Leaf Gardens on September 6, 1964, flash bulbs went off, blinding everyone, and the roar of 16,761 screaming voices made it impossible to hear the music, blinding and deafening the band. Items like bras and lipsticks rained down, leading to 109 fans fainting at the venue, described as "mass hysteria" rather than just a rock show. "It's unclear if they could even hear their own voices over the roar of 16,761 streaming voices, nor do we know if they could see anything as bras, lipsticks, and other items rain down on them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Massive Police Deployment in Toronto (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' first visit to Toronto in September 1964 necessitated an extraordinary police response, with more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario Provincial Police, and the counties called in. By noon, 4,000 police officers and auxiliaries were on duty around Maple Leaf Gardens, dividing the crowd into smaller sections, with majestic horses used to push back waves of "deranged youth." "The band's first visit to Toronto required more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario provincial police, and the counties."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mayor Phil Givens Snubbed (1964)
podcast.body: On September 6, 1964, Toronto mayor Phil Givens and his wife attempted to visit The Beatles at the King Edward Hotel at 1:30 pm but were turned away by a "blonde woman." She claimed two of the Beatles were sleeping and two were with relatives, an incident that led to the Daily Star publishing an article with the headline, "Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor." "The next day, the daily star released an article with the headline, Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Montreal Arrival and Death Threats (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' arrival at Dorval Airport for their only visit to La Belle province mirrored the scenes at other tour stops, with hordes of screaming fans. However, their time in Quebec was significantly marred by death threats from French Canadian separatists, specifically the FLQ, leading to the presence of police sharpshooters at the Montreal Forum on St. Catherine Street for their two concerts. "Their arrival at the Dorval Airport mirrored what happened at every stop on their tour. Hordes of screaming fans at the airport throngs of fans lying the streets, clutching magazines and singing their favorite Beatles songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Opening Acts Booed by Impatient Crowd (1964)
podcast.body: At the Maple Leaf Gardens concert in Toronto on September 6, 1964, the opening bands, which included Bill Black's Combo, The Exciters, Clarence "Frogman" Henry, and Jackie De Shannon, were met with boos from the crowd. The audience was impatient and made it clear they wanted only one band: The Beatles. "As the opening bands, which included Bill Black's combo, the exciders Clarence Frogman Henry, and the Celterie Jackie De Shannon hit the stage to crowd-bood, they only wanted one band, and one band only."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pan Am Flight 101 Arrival - February 7, 1964
podcast.body: The band's arrival on Pan Am Flight 101 from London at JFK Airport in New York on February 7, 1964, symbolized a massive explosion of Britishness and national pride. This event was referenced as a benchmark for the level of national pride seen again during the Britpop era. "an explosion of pride in Britishness that we really hadn't seen since February 7, 1964 when Pan Am Flight 101 from London touched down at JFK Airport in New York carrying a band called The Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Paul McCartney Greets Winnipeg (1964)
podcast.body: Following the incident with Bryce Decker at the Winnipeg airport on August 18, 1964, Paul McCartney exited the plane, yelled "Hello, Winnipeg," and descended the stairs, where he was immediately swarmed by a throng of reporters, including Bob Burns. This brief appearance was the band's only direct interaction with the Winnipeg crowd, as they never returned to the city. "Oh, and the man who greeted the crowd was none other than Paul McCartney."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peaceful Departure from Toronto (1964)
podcast.body: The day after their chaotic concerts, just before noon on September 7, 1964, The Beatles headed back to the Toronto airport. The sun was shining, the crowd was considerably smaller than the previous day, and the mood was distinctly different. The band signed autographs, posed for photos, waved to their admirers, and then boarded their plane, marking the end of their first Toronto visit. "The sun was shining, and the crowd was considerably smaller. The mood was also different. This was the end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Concert Activities and Press Conference (1964)
podcast.body: After their first concert at Maple Leaf Gardens ended around 6 pm on September 6, 1964, The Beatles were quickly moved to a dressing room. There, they took photographs with local DJs, fan club presidents, and Miss Canada, followed by a press conference where they appeared somewhat bewildered but maintained their charming demeanor and "savage wit" towards journalists. "They then had a press conference where they looked a little bewildered, but as usual they were charming to admirers, and unleashed their savage wit on journalists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ringo Starr's Worry Over Montreal Threats (1964)
podcast.body: Ringo Starr expressed genuine worry about the death threats received during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal concerts. He recalled that some individuals targeted him "as an English Jew," despite him not being Jewish, noting that while threats were often taken "in stride," this particular incident, despite more police presence, was one of the few times he was truly concerned. "Some people decided to make an example of me as an English Jew. The one major fault is, I'm not Jewish. Threats we took in stride. I mean, suddenly there'd be a few more cops, but this was one of the few times I was really worried."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rock's Rescuers (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles are credited with rescuing rock music after a period of decline, creating a widespread "tsunami" that influenced music for the remainder of the 1960s. "The Beatles, of course, rescued Rock, created this tsunami that spread across the planet, and it lasted the rest of the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Significant Chart Competition (1964)
podcast.body: In 1964, The Beatles emerged as formidable competition for The Beach Boys. They famously occupied the number one, two, and three spots on the charts at a time when The Beach Boys' "Fun, Fun, Fun" peaked at number five, prompting Brian Wilson to intensify his creative efforts. "But the group suddenly had some real competition, and numbers one, two and three were the Beatles."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Vancouver Concert Delay and Paperwork (1964)
podcast.body: The Beatles' Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, was scheduled for 8 pm, but a significant delay occurred because the pilot of their plane forgot to sign a required document. This forced the band to return to the airport to complete the paperwork, while 20,000 fans impatiently waited at the stadium. "The show was supposed to start at 8pm, but the pilot of the plane bringing the Beatles to Canada forgot to sign a document, and the band was forced to return to the airport to finish the paperwork and then head back to the stadium."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Best New Artist Win (1965)
podcast.body: The Beatles were awarded Best New Artist in 1965, which was described as a "mild acknowledgement of Beatlemania," indicating a gradual shift in Grammy recognition towards youth-directed pop. "They did give best new artist to the group in 1965, a mild acknowledgement of Beatlemania."

podcast.body: The Beatles were highly active and influential in 1965, contributing significantly to a prolific year for rock music and its role as an agent for social change. "the Beatles and everything they were doing"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Promotional Films (1965)
podcast.body: By 1965, The Beatles were exhausted by the constant demand for live performances on radio and television. They sought a way to appear on TV without physically being present. Their solution was to create promotional film clips for songs like "We Can Work It Out" and "Day Tripper," shot in November 1965, and subsequently "I Feel Fine," "Ticket to Ride," and "Help!". These clips were then distributed to anyone requesting a Beatles performance, setting a precedent for promotional videos. "The Beatles were tired of the grind of performing on radio and TV. But if there was a way to appear on TV, without having to appear on TV."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: Northern Songs Becomes Publicly Traded (1965)
podcast.body: Two years after its inception, Northern Songs became a publicly traded company. At this point, Ringo Starr and George Harrison received small stakes in the business, though they were reportedly unhappy with their share. "Two years later, Northern Songs became a publicly traded company. At this point, Ringo and George also got small stakes in the business."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return to Toronto and Fading Beatlemania (1965)
podcast.body: On August 17, 1965, The Beatles returned to Canada, flying in from New York to Pearson Airport (then Toronto International Airport), where fans again rushed them, met by Toronto police. They stayed at the King Edward Hotel, where "smart fans" booked dozens of rooms. However, the enthusiasm had waned slightly, as newspaper coverage shifted from front-page headlines to inside pages, with many suggesting that Beatlemania was fading and the band's popularity might soon disappear. "Unlike the previous year when the band made front page news in Toronto, this year, they were on the inside pages, with many starting to say that Biddlemania was fading, and the band would soon disappear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shea Stadium Sound Disaster (1965)
podcast.body: When The Beatles played Shea Stadium on August 15, 1965, there was no proper concert sound system for the venue. They set up on a small stage, using a bunch of mics and a couple of 100 Watt Vox amplifiers, and pumped everything through the stadium's public address system—the same speakers and amplifiers used for baseball announcements. It was so bad that the Beatles not only couldn't be heard by the audience but also couldn't hear themselves. "As a last second fix, one of the road crew flipped over some of their amplifiers and pointed them directly at the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift Towards Album as Artistic Statement (Circa 1965)
podcast.body: Around 1965, prominent artists such as The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and The Beach Boys began to pivot from focusing on individual singles towards conceptualizing albums as complete artistic statements, typically comprising ten, twelve, or more interconnected tracks. "But starting in around 1965, a number of artists, the Beatles, Bob Dylan, and the Beach Boys among them, began to think less in terms of individual songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shifting Album Perception (c. 1965)
podcast.body: Around 1965, The Beatles, alongside Bob Dylan and others, began to view the album as a medium for artistic expression, leading them to write longer, more complex, and carefully sequenced collections of songs rather than just single-focused releases. "The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and a few others looked at the album and thought, I can work with this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "More Popular Than Jesus" Controversy (1966)
podcast.body: In 1966, John Lennon's casual comment that The Beatles were "more popular than Jesus" ignited a significant controversy. Broadcasters Tommy Charles and Doug Layton in Birmingham, Alabama, initiated a campaign to ban The Beatles over this perceived blasphemy, leading to numerous records being broken and publicly burned. "And when John Lennon made a flippin' comment in 1966 about the Beatles being more popular than Jesus, two broadcasters, Tommy Charles and Doug Layton from Birmingham, Alabama, started a campaign to ban the Beatles over this blasphemy, and many records were broken and burned."

podcast.title: Departure from Canada (1966)
podcast.body: After their final concerts in Toronto on August 17, 1966, The Beatles stayed overnight before flying out to Boston on August 18th. This departure marked their definitive farewell to Canadian stages, as they never toured again. "This time, they left forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early End to Touring (1966)
podcast.body: Following the terrible sound experience at Shea Stadium in 1965, where they were miserable due to not being able to hear themselves, The Beatles played their last proper live gig a year later. The severe issues with concert sound reinforcement directly contributed to their decision to never tour again. "A year later, they played their last proper live gig, and they never toured again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Toronto Concerts (1966)
podcast.body: On August 17, 1966, The Beatles performed their last Canadian concerts in Toronto, with 15,000 fans attending the first show and 17,000 for the second at 8 pm. Bill J. Nelson served as MC, and the routine chaos continued, with 50 audience members treated for shock and screaming volumes making the music barely audible. "That number only went up to 17,000 fans for their second concert at 8pm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Invitation to Last Tour (1966)
podcast.body: The Beatles invited The Ronettes to be their support act on their final tour in 1966. However, Phil Spector's insistence that Ronnie remain in the studio led to her cousin Elaine substituting, which reportedly disappointed The Beatles. "Also in 1966, the Runettes were invited by the Beatles to be their support act on their last ever tour, but once again Spectre insisted that Ronnie couldn't go because she needed to be in the studio, so Elaine substituted for her again, much to the Beatles' disappointment."

srcs.episode: Episode 110: "Be My Baby" by the Ronettes

podcast.title: Last Canadian and Touring Concerts (1966)
podcast.body: The Beatles returned to Canada on August 17, 1966, for their final two concerts ever on Canadian soil in Toronto. This tour also marked the last time the band would ever play live, consisting of only eight shows over 12 days before they stopped touring forever to focus exclusively on studio music. "Just a year later in 1966, the band returned for their last two concerts ever on Canadian soil. The tour was also the last the band would ever play."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-1966 Studio Band Fades
podcast.body: After 1966, when The Beatles stopped touring and evolved into a studio band, they frequently incorporated fade-outs into their songs. This allowed them to avoid crafting a definitive ending for a live audience, opting instead for an artistic or technical fade. "The Beatles were big into the fade after 1966 when they stopped touring and became a studio band and no longer had to properly finish a song for a live audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dick James Sells Share to ATV Music (Post-1967)
podcast.body: After Brian Epstein's death in 1967, The Beatles' business affairs became chaotic. Relations with Dick James soured, leading him to sell his share of Northern Songs to ATV Music without informing John Lennon and Paul McCartney, who were upset and attempted unsuccessfully to buy James's share themselves. "After Manager Brian Epstein died in 1967, the business affairs of the Beatles were in shambles. Relations between the group and Dick James music soured, and Dick James wanted out of Northern Songs. That's when he sold his share to a company called ATV Music without giving any notice to John and Paul."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Public Performance (1969)
podcast.body: On January 30, 1969, the four members of The Beatles performed together for the last time on the rooftop of the Apple Records building. This spontaneous concert marked a significant moment in the band's history. "el 30 de enero de 1969 en la zoteada de Apple Records tocarían juntos por última vez los Beatles."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: 1970 Breakup and Lasting Influence
podcast.body: The Beatles broke up in 1970, yet they are still considered the greatest and most influential rock group of all time, maintaining their status indefinitely. "Even though they broke up in 1970, they are still the greatest and most influential rock group of all time and will probably be forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Beatles Sell Their Share to ATV Music (By January 1970)
podcast.body: Following a dispute with ATV over their publishing share, and after their manager Allen Klein failed to secure the desired deal, The Beatles sold their remaining stake in Northern Songs to ATV Music. By January 1970, ATV owned 99% of The Beatles' publishing. This financial tension significantly contributed to the band's breakup a few months later. "Very, very long story short, they did not get the deal they wanted, so the Beatles sold their piece of Northern Songs to ATV. By January 1970, ATV owned 99% of the Beatles' publishing. This financial tension went a long ways towards the Beatles breaking up a few months later."

podcast.body: In 1972, The Osmonds achieved 11 gold records, a feat that surpassed the record for most gold records in a single year, even unmatched by The Beatles at that time. "At that time that was a record unmatched by even the Beatles or Elvis."

"By 1980, under supervision from the Kremlin, state recording company Melodia, started bootlegging recordings by the Beatles and the Rolling Stones."

podcast.title: Delayed Adoption of CD Format (1983-1987)
podcast.body: When compact discs emerged in early 1983, The Beatles' organization was highly cautious, delaying their entry into the new format until early 1987 to observe its market development and stability. "When the compact disc started showing up in stores in early 1983, the Beatles would have none of this new format."

podcast.title: Initial CD Releases and Liner Notes (1983)
podcast.body: When CDs first launched in 1983, initial releases, including some of The Beatles' albums, often came with "wretched" and uninspired liner note booklets. These early CD packages frequently featured minimal content, sometimes just a small piece of glossy paper with one side blank, falling short of the detailed liner notes seen on vinyl LPs. "Some of the first Beatles albums released on CD came this way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Michael Jackson Outbids McCartney for ATV Music (1985)
podcast.body: Following advice from Paul McCartney in 1983 about the value of publishing ("He who owns the publishing controls the world"), Michael Jackson purchased ATV Music, which included 250 Beatles songs (nearly everything they wrote) and tracks by The Rolling Stones, Elvis, and Bruce Springsteen, for $47.5 million. He outbid McCartney, who was reportedly displeased. "In 1983, McCartney was doing some work with Michael Jackson, and they got to talking about business affairs. The money is in publishing, Mac and console Jacko. He who owns the publishing controls the world. And this was advice that Jackson never forgot. In 1985, ATV Music, that company with the Beatles publishing, went up for sale. Four thousand songs, including 250 from the Beatles, which is pretty much everything they ever wrote, as well as tracks by the Rolling Stones, Elvis and Bruce Springsteen. Jackson then outbid McCartney, paying $47.5 million for this catalog. Maca was not pleased."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: CD Adoption Holdouts (1987)
podcast.body: The Beatles were among the holdouts in adopting the compact disc format, with their catalog not coming to CD until 1987. "The Beatles didn't come on stream until 1987."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nike Commercial Controversy (1987)
podcast.body: The use of "Revolution" in a 1987 Nike sneaker commercial sparked a major controversy in the music world, with the media extensively criticizing it as the "ultimate sellout of baby boomer musical iconography." This reaction occurred despite the approval of the song's use by Michael Jackson, who owned its publishing, and reportedly by Yoko Ono. "Jackson then owned the Beatles publishing, and he approved the sale of the song for use in the ad for half a million dollars."

podcast.title: George Harrison on Ringo's Death Threat (1990)
podcast.body: In 1990, George Harrison recounted a specific death threat against Ringo Starr during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal visit. He stated that a Montreal newspaper reported someone intended to kill Ringo, possibly because they disliked his nose or because he was perceived as "the most British of the Beatles." "A Montreal newspaper reported that somebody was going to kill Ringo because they didn't like his nose or something, because he was probably the most British of the Beatles."

podcast.title: Michael Jackson Sells Half of Catalog to Sony Music (1995)
podcast.body: Facing financial issues, Michael Jackson sold half of his ATV Music catalog to Sony Music for approximately $100 million, generating a significant return on his investment. "Fast forward to 1995. Jackson was having financial issues, so he sold half of this catalog to Sony Music for about $100 million."

podcast.title: Boycott of Digital Music Stores (2003-2010)
podcast.body: The Beatles, having been significant victims of music piracy, initially boycotted digital music distribution. Their songs and albums only became legally available on the iTunes Music Store (launched 2003) and other digital platforms on November 16, 2010, seven years after iTunes' debut. "The iTunes music store went online April 28, 2003, but the Beatles, victims of music piracy more than most, boxed."

podcast.title: George Harrison Memorial Tree (2004)
podcast.body: In 2004, a tree was planted in Griffith Park in Los Angeles and dedicated to the memory of George Harrison, who was known for his love of gardening. After growing to over 10 feet tall, the tree was tragically attacked and killed by a species of tree beetle, creating an ironic situation where a "Beatle tree was killed by a tree beetle." "Therefore, a beetle tree was killed by a tree beetle."

podcast.title: Sony Acquires Larger Share, Catalog Valued at $1 Billion (2006)
podcast.body: In 2006, due to continued financial difficulties for Jackson, Sony retained an option to buy an additional 50% of Jackson's remaining share in the catalog. This would have given Sony 75% ownership of The Beatles' publishing, with the catalog then valued at about $1 billion. "In 2006, Jacko was having more financial issues, so Sony retained an option to buy 50% of Jackson's remaining share. So that means Sony would own 75% of the Beatles publishing. And at that point, the catalog was valued at about $1 billion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Symbolic Endorsement of Digital Distribution (2010, 2015)
podcast.body: The Beatles' eventual decision to make their music available on iTunes (2010) and then streaming services (2015) was viewed by many in the music industry as a crucial legitimization of these digital trends, given their status as "the biggest band the world has ever seen." "Since among many people inside and outside the music industry, was that none of these trends or technologies were fully operational and legitimate, unless the Beatles, the biggest band the world has ever seen, embraced them."

podcast.title: Boycott of Streaming Services (Pre-2015)
podcast.body: The Beatles extended their cautious approach to streaming platforms, withholding their music from all legal streaming services until Christmas Eve 2015, long after other artists had embraced the format. "No platform could legally stream any Beatles song until Christmas Eve 2015."

podcast.title: George Martin's Death in 2016

podcast.body: After Michael Jackson's death in 2009, the remainder of the catalog transferred to his estate. In 2016, his estate sold the rest of his shares in ATV Music to Sony for $750 million. "Then Jackson dies in 2009. The remainder of the catalog transfers to Jackson's estate. And in 2016, the rest of his shares in ATV Music are sold to Sony for $750 million."

podcast.title: Paul McCartney Regains Control of His Music (2017)
podcast.body: In 2017, after launching a lawsuit related to a new American copyright law, a court ruled in Paul McCartney's favor, allowing him to regain control of his music after 50 years. "Two years later, Paul McCartney comes back in, launches a lawsuit related to a new American copyright law. And in 2017, a court ruled in his favor. So after 50 years, Paul McCartney finally regains control of his music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Her Majesty" - Accidental Hidden Track
podcast.body: The inclusion of "Her Majesty" as a hidden track on "Abbey Road" was an unintended consequence of studio procedure. After Paul McCartney requested the song's removal, tape assistant John Kerlander snipped it out and spliced it to the end of the master tape with 20 seconds of blank tape, in accordance with Abbey Road's rules for edited material. A mastering engineer either overlooked or misread Kerlander's note, resulting in the song's presence on the final master, which the Beatles found "really cool" and decided to keep. "And so the first hidden track came to be as the result of an accident."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Lady Madonna Piano" at Abbey Road
podcast.body: Located in Abbey Road Studio 2, there is a beat-up upright piano with a sign that explicitly reads "Lady Madonna Piano. Do not touch." This piano is a notable artifact from The Beatles' time recording there. "You pass a beat up upright piano, which has a sign on top. And that sign reads, Lady Madonna Piano. Do not touch."

podcast.title: "Long Tall Sally" Cover Influence
podcast.body: At a Paris concert in January 1964, Arthur Howes observed the "biggest reaction" to The Beatles' cover version of Little Richard's "Long Tall Sally." This observation prompted Howes to suggest The Kinks record the song as their debut single, believing it would be a guaranteed hit for someone. "Howes was in Paris with the Beatles in January 1964, and he noticed that one of the songs that was getting the biggest reaction was their cover version of Little Richard's Long-Tall Sally."

Film director Peter Jackson was able to isolate John Lennon's vocals from a "bad sounding 1978 cassette demo," allowing Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr to add new parts, alongside George Harrison's contributions from a 1995 session. podcast.body: The Beatles were part of the thriving British music scene in the 1960s. However, despite their popularity, it was challenging to hear their music on British radio due to the lack of legal private commercial radio and the BBC's policies at the time. "Britain was exploding with music in the 1960s with the Beatles and the Stones and so on, it was pretty much impossible to hear those British bands on British radio."

podcast.body: The Beatles were a significant musical entity that defined the 1960s, contributing to the era's musical landscape alongside the rise of the album format and megagrock festivals. "The 1960s brought us the Beatles, the Rise of the Album, the Megarock Festival."

podcast.title: 50th Anniversary Box Set Remastering Series
podcast.body: Between approximately 2017 and 2022, Apple Records released a series of 50th-anniversary collections of classic Beatles albums. These sets featured the original albums remastered by Giles Martin, the son of famed Beatles producer George Martin. Giles Martin's process involved going back to the original master tapes to deconstruct and reconstruct each album, aiming to make it sound as much like the original as possible but with a fresher quality and improved stereo separation, as stereo technology was new in the 1960s. Albums released in this series included *Sgt. Pepper*, *The White Album*, *Abbey Road*, *Let It Be*, and *Revolver*. "Apple Records, the Beatles still existent label, was putting out these collections, these 50th anniversary collections, where the classic Beatles albums were remastered by Giles Martin."

This led to the invention of Automatic Double Tracking (ADT) specifically for him, allowing a single vocal take to be automatically doubled with a slight delay. podcast.title: EMI Audition Demo (Undated) – "Hello Little Girl" / "Till There Was You" Acetate
podcast.body: A one-of-a-kind, 10-inch acetate test pressing recorded as an audition for EMI Records, representing the first record featuring the Beatles as they would become known. Side A features "Hello Little Girl," credited to Paul McCartney and the Beatles, while Side B has "Till There Was You," credited to John Lennon and the Beatles; manager Brian Epstein wrote the titles in blue pen to ensure fairness. This record disappeared for decades before being found in the attic of Les Maguire, a member of Gerry and the Pacemakers. It was sold in March 2016 for 77,500 pounds, equivalent to $95,000 American or $130,000 Canadian. "It's a 10-inch acetate, a test pressing in other words, and is a one-of-a-kind thing Hello Little Girl on the A side, and Till There Was You on the B side."

podcast.body: At just 18 years old, John Kerlander worked as a tape assistant at Abbey Road Studios. He was responsible for compiling the rough mixes for the 16-minute medley featured on side two of the "Abbey Road" album. His adherence to studio rules regarding excised material led to the accidental creation of the first hidden track, "Her Majesty." "A guy with a name of John Kerlander was a tape assistant at Abby Road Studios. podcast.body: John Lennon's songs will remain with Sony until 70 years after his death, meaning his heirs will not benefit from the income until after 2050. podcast.title: Loss of Publishing Rights
podcast.body: The Beatles notoriously lost control over a significant portion of their songs, specifically those released before 1966. This occurred due to various publishing deals signed as new artists, preventing them from earning money from many of their early hits. "It's how the Beatles managed to lose control of a vast number of their songs, biggest band ever, and they weren't making money from so many of their songs that they released before 1966."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Mainstream Artist
podcast.body: The Beatles were listed as an example of a "big, famous band" on "big major labels." These artists represented the mainstream, achieving millions in record and ticket sales, widespread media coverage, and global household recognition. "They signed bands like Led Zeppelin and the Stones and the Beatles and ACDC and Van Halen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Management Crisis and Disagreement (Post-Epstein)
podcast.body: After the death of their manager Brian Epstein, The Beatles faced a management crisis. Three members of the band favored appointing Rolling Stones manager Alan Klein to handle their affairs. However, Paul McCartney wished to work with his father-in-law, Lee Eastman, an entertainment lawyer who managed the finances of many musicians. This fundamental disagreement over management created significant tension within the group. "And that tension, that disagreement went a long way towards ending the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manufactured Rivalry with The Rolling Stones
podcast.body: The widely perceived rivalry between The Beatles and The Rolling Stones was largely manufactured by the media. In reality, the members of both bands were very good friends. "The Beatles versus the Stones, although that was a manufactured fight. They were actually very good friends."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marine Worm Species
podcast.body: A marine worm species, *Grifiela Bidli*, was named after The Beatles. The scientists were reminded of the Beatles' distinctive haircuts by the worm's shaggy fur. "It has Shaggy Fur, which seemed to remind scientists of the Beatles' haircuts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Master Tape Degradation
podcast.body: A significant portion of The Beatles' discography, particularly their final master tapes recorded on wide-spectrum electromagnetic tape, has suffered severe degradation and erasure over time. These vital original recordings no longer exist due to the inherent progressive degradation of magnetic tapes. "tenemos una parte importante a escografía de los Beatles que los más tercera y finales en cinta de tromagneticado en deba que se deterioraron si se borraron y ya no existen."

podcast.title: Mono Recording Practice
podcast.body: The Beatles consistently recorded their music in mono up until the release of "The White Album." This practice was common before stereo became the industry standard, leading to many mono masters being later converted to "fake stereo" for commercial release. "The Beatles, for example, recorded in mono all the way through to the white album."

podcast.title: Mono Reissues Revival
podcast.body: Mono records from the pre-1968 era, including reissues from The Beatles, were noted for making a comeback and sounding particularly good. "They sound really good to check out the Beatles reissues on mono."

podcast.title: Mop Top Hairstyle Adoption
podcast.body: The Beatles introduced their distinctive "mop top" haircuts, which served as an initial step in the trend of men's hair growing longer throughout the 1960s. This style was a key part of signaling membership in the counterculture movement. "When the Beatles showed up with their mop tops, that was just the start."

podcast.body: The Beatles are mentioned as an example of a band whose sound was explicitly *not* the lineage from which "alternative" music of the early 90s (like grunge) descended, distinguishing it from punk and new wave. podcast.title: Origin of Mop Top Haircut (Yurgen Volmer)
podcast.body: In 1961, Paul McCartney and John Lennon met Yurgen Volmer in Paris, who was a friend of Astrid Kircher and Stu Sutcliffe. Volmer had long hair parted and worn over his forehead, which "entranced" Lennon and McCartney, who still wore their hair slicked back. They asked him to cut their hair in his style, giving birth to the first version of the Beatles' mop top. "So he cut their hair, and so the Beatles' mop top was born, or at least the first version of it."

podcast.title: Origin of Sergeant Pepper Mustaches
podcast.body: In late 1966, all members of The Beatles began growing mustaches, a fashion choice prominently featured on the artwork for their "Sergeant Pepper" album the following year. This trend originated after Paul McCartney had a moped crash, resulting in a face injury and a scar on his lip from bad stitches. He grew a mustache to conceal the scar, and the rest of the band followed suit. "Paul McCarty had a crash on a moat pad, which resulted in a faceplant on the pavement and this left a scar on his lip due to some bad stitches. And he became self-conscious of the scar. He grew a mustache and the rest of the band followed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Mono vs. Re-channeled Stereo Recordings
podcast.body: In A/B comparisons, the original mono masters of The Beatles' recordings are often perceived as sounding better than their re-channeled stereo counterparts. This is because the mono versions represent how the music was originally recorded and engineered, prior to the artificial stereo conversion processes. "if you've ever done A, B comparisons between those re-channeled Beatles recordings and the original mono masters, you probably believe that the mono recordings sound better, because that's how they were recorded and that's how they were engineered."

podcast.title: Overall Influence

podcast.body: Paul McCartney conceived the initial idea for Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band as a way to invent a new band identity that wasn't The Beatles. podcast.title: Paul McCartney's Shock and Subsequent Catalog Acquisitions
podcast.body: Paul McCartney was "especially stunned" by the loss of his Beatles' publishing rights. This experience motivated him to invest heavily in music catalogs, beginning in 1973 with the purchase of Norvat Jack Music, which included songs by his idol Buddy Holly, establishing a significant income stream from controlled catalogs. "Paul McCartney was especially stunned by this. He learned the hard way about the value of owning the publishing-depository music. So if he couldn't own his own music, the music he made with the Beatles, he decided that he would bulk up his financial holdings by buying the catalogs of others. He started in 1973 buying a company called Norvat Jack Music, which contained many of the songs by Buddy Holly"

podcast.body: The band experienced an incident with the First Lady of the Philippines, which led to them having to abandon the country. podcast.title: Pioneer of the Matched Grip
podcast.body: Ringo Starr significantly influenced new drummers by popularizing the "matched grip" for holding drum sticks. Traditionally, drummers used the "jazz grip," with one stick held like a club and the other from underneath with the palm facing upward. Ringo favored holding both sticks like clubs, allowing drummers to "attack their instrument" with more energy and a primal feel. His appearances on Ed Sullivan and in movies during the mid-1960s led almost every subsequent rock drummer to adopt the matched grip. "Ringo favorite the matched grip, where both sticks were held like clubs."

podcast.title: Pioneering 12-String Rickenbacker Use
podcast.body: After The Searchers' "Needles and Pins" created an electric 12-string sound, both The Searchers and The Beatles regularly started using 12-string Rickenbackers to achieve a similar sound. "soon both they and the Beatles would be regularly using 12 string rick and backers to get the same sound."

podcast.title: Pioneering Albums as an Art Form
podcast.body: The Beatles, alongside Bob Dylan, are credited with making music more sophisticated and releasing albums that were taken seriously, similar to jazz, classical, or Broadway recordings. "Credit can go to the Beatles and Bob Dylan because not only was their music much more sophisticated, but they also released albums."

podcast.title: Pioneering Melodies and Arrangements
podcast.body: The Beatles remain popular because they were among the first to develop many great melodies and arrangements, establishing a foundational influence in popular music. These films were sent to TV networks as an alternative to live performances on music shows in the UK and across Europe, a practice later adopted by MTV. "This was pioneered by the Beatles, as far back as the middle 1960s."

podcast.title: Refusal to Play Encores
podcast.body: The Beatles famously never played encores during their performances. This was attributed to the overwhelming nature of their crowds, which were so frantic that the band would complete their set and immediately escape in a waiting car. "The Beatles never played Encore's. They couldn't. The crowds were so crazy that they played their set and escaped in a waiting car."

podcast.title: Rejection by Joe Meek
podcast.body: In their early days, The Beatles' demo tape was presented to Joe Meek by Brian Epstein, who sought Meek's professional advice on managing the budding band. Meek famously dismissed their talent, unequivocally advising Epstein against representing them. "Brian Epstein, amigo de Mick, demostró una maqueta de una banda que estaba empezando para pedirle consejos sobre si representarle sonó. La banda se llamaba Beatles, la respuesta de Mick fue que Nisemo le estáse."

podcast.body: Prior to recording Sgt. Pepper's, The Beatles had already stopped performing live and were disinclined to return to the stage. This decision allowed them to focus on studio work that was not necessarily reproducible in concerts. "ellos ya directamente no podían más, habían madurado, estaban inmersos en una cultura que los dominaba y que los movía como si fuese en títeres."

podcast.title: Ringo Starr's Gregarious Nature
podcast.body: Bob Burns, the CJAYTV reporter who announced The Beatles' arrival in Winnipeg and interviewed John Lennon, later stated that Ringo Starr was the most gregarious member of the band and appeared to be the most mature. "He would later state that Ringo Star was the most gregarious of the band and seemed the most mature."

podcast.title: Ringo Starr's Songwriting Contributions
podcast.body: Contrary to a common misconception that Ringo Starr composed songs he sang, he did not begin writing songs for The Beatles until *The White Album* (1968), where he penned "Don't Pass Me By." His only other composition for the band was "Octopus's Garden" on *Abbey Road* (1969). Before this, John Lennon and Paul McCartney frequently wrote songs for Ringo to sing, such as "A Little Help from My Friends," and he also sang cover tracks like Buck Owens' "Act Naturally." "Ringo didn't start writing songs until the white album when he wrote Don't Pass Me By."

podcast.title: Ringo Starr's White Album (0000001) Sale
podcast.body: Ringo Starr owned the unique copy of _The White Album_ bearing the serial number 0000001. He sold this highly sought-after collectible for charity in 2015, fetching $790,000. "It was Ringo Star who had number 00001. And he sold it off for charity in 2015 for $790,000."

podcast.body: The Beatles' rivalry with The Rolling Stones in the 1960s is characterized as a "gentleman's game," differing significantly from the intense hatred between Blur and Oasis in the Britpop era, as The Beatles and The Stones were "actually mates." podcast.body: The Beatles are among the artists who have experienced "second chance hits" or "bringbacks," where singles initially flopped or did nothing on the charts before a catalyst propelled them to smash success. podcast.title: Seven-Year Transformation
podcast.body: In just seven years, The Beatles managed to change everything across all genres of music, establishing themselves as a powerful and influential force. "The Beatles changed everything across all genres, and they did it in just seven years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift Towards Album-Oriented Music
podcast.body: Around 1965, The Beatles, along with Bob Dylan and others, began to view the album as a creative medium, writing longer and more complex songs and carefully sequenced collections of tracks. This marked a turning point away from the singles-dominated music landscape.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift from Singles to Albums
podcast.body: The Beatles played a pivotal role in shifting music commerce in the 1960s from a focus on singles to a focus on full-length albums. The album *Revolver* is considered a key pivot point for this change, occurring just before *Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band*. "I talked about how the Beatles kind of shifted music commerce from the single to the album in the 60s. And, you know, revolver is kind of the pivot point for that, just before Sargent Pepper."

podcast.title: Signature Ludwig Kit
podcast.body: Ringo Starr played a standard four-piece Ludwig drum kit, notable for its oyster gray finish. This particular setup, consisting of a snare, bass drum, mounted tom, and floor tom, became an influential template for many drummers. "He played a standard four-piece Ludwig kit with an oyster gray finish."

podcast.title: Singing X-Rated Lyrics Live
podcast.body: Due to the overwhelming noise from screaming fans and inadequate PA equipment, The Beatles often found it impossible to be heard during their live performances. To cope with their frustration, they would sometimes sing X-rated lyrics instead of the original words to songs such as "A Hard Day's Night" and "I Want to Hold Your Hand." "The Beatles handled their frustration by singing X-rated lyrics to some of their songs when they performed."

podcast.title: Singles on Pocket Discs
podcast.body: The Beatles' singles were made available on Pocket Discs through a partnership between Ameracom and Apple Records. These discs were sold for 50 cents each in vending machines. `"They were sold only in vending machines, 50 cents a pop, and they teamed with Apple records, meaning that you could buy Beatles singles this way."`

podcast.title: Soviet Soundalikes
podcast.body: After 1964, the first Soviet rock groups often emerged as soundalikes of The Beatles and The Rolling Stones, indicating the significant influence these Western bands had on early Soviet rock musicians. These groups were categorized as either "official, vocal, instrumental assemblies" or "unofficial amateurs." "The first Soviet rock groups were beetles and stone soundalikes, emerging after 1964."

podcast.title: Soviet X-Ray Records (Ribs)
podcast.body: During the era when Western records were banned in the Soviet Union, songs by The Beatles were among the most highly sought-after recordings found on black market X-ray records, known as "ribs." "Today, people collect these ribs, especially of songs by the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, Elvis, and the Beach Boys, as well as other Western artists."

podcast.title: Stance Against Inferior B-sides
podcast.body: The Beatles consciously chose not to put inferior material on the B-sides of their singles. They aimed to provide fans with maximum value, leading to the creation of what became known as double A-sides, where both tracks were considered equally important. "The Beatles, for example, came to issue putting something inferior on the B side of their singles. They wanted to give fans as much value as they possibly could."

podcast.title: State-Sanctioned Bootlegging
podcast.body: By 1980, under the supervision of the Kremlin, the Soviet state recording company Melodia began officially bootlegging recordings by The Beatles and The Rolling Stones. This act of intellectual property theft was, ironically, seen as furthering the CIA's objective of distributing Western music and soft power within the USSR. "By 1980, under supervision from the Kremlin, state recording company Melodia, started bootlegging recordings by the Beatles and the Rolling Stones."

podcast.title: Target of "Screaming Mania"
podcast.body: The Beatles became the subject of widespread "Beetlemania," with their female fans screaming intensely at their performances. This phenomenon followed earlier instances of screaming fans for Rudy Vallée and Frank Sinatra, marking a generational continuation of fervent fan devotion. "The next generation, the daughters of Valley fans, latched onto Frank Sinatra, and the grand daughters became screaming Beetlemaniacs."

podcast.title: Target of Religious Condemnation
podcast.body: The Beatles were identified as a prime target during the 1950s when religious leaders widely condemned Rock and Roll as "the music of the devil," immoral, and evil. "Elvis and the Beatles were two prime targets."

It is acceptable for listeners to appreciate bands like The Beatles alongside more extreme genres such as death metal from Norway, indicating a breakdown of traditional musical "silos." concerts.title: Shakespeare Stadium (August 1965)
concerts.body: The Beatles performed at Shakespeare Stadium in August 1965, during which their amplification system proved insufficient for the crowd's noise. They used four All-Tech amplifiers, each generating 175 watts, through the stadium's baseball PA system. Despite this being considered "crazy, crazy loud" at the time, the crowd generated 135 decibels of noise, which was twice the volume the amps could produce, highlighting the critical need for improved concert amplification. "When The Beatles played Shakespeare Stadium in August 1965, all they had behind them was four all-tech amplifiers, each generating 175 watts of power, through the same PA system that the announcer used for baseball games."

xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957)
xref.body: Ringo Starr, born on July 7, 1940, was exempt from compulsory national service in Britain. This exemption, due to the end of the obligation in 1957 for those born after October 1, 1939, allowed him to focus on music. "And future Beatles Ringo Starr was born on July 7, 1940."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
xref.body: The end of compulsory national service in Britain in 1957 (for those born after Oct 1, 1939) and its complete abolition in November 1960 meant that young men in bands like The Quarrymen were exempt from military service. This freedom allowed members like John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940), and by implication, all four future Beatles, to continue pursuing music rather than being drafted. "And that meant that the young men in a new group called the Corrie men wouldn't have to worry about going into the army, so they kept at it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
xref.body: All four members of The Beatles managed to avoid compulsory national service in Britain, which ended in 1957 for those born on or after October 1, 1939, and was completely abolished in November 1960. John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940) were specifically mentioned as being exempt. This allowed them and countless other young British men to dedicate their time to forming bands and playing music, directly contributing to the explosion of the British music scene and the British Invasion. "And in November 1960, when compulsory service ended all together, all four members of the Beatles managed to avoid going into the army."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Beatles' Release Strategy (1963-1965)
xref.body: During 1963-1965, The Beatles employed a prolific release strategy, putting out up to a dozen singles per year, which were then consolidated into two annual albums, a model cited as a precedent for the constant flow of new music required from artists today. "Artists need to deliver a constant flow of new songs, just like the Beatles did through the year 1963, 64 and 65, when they'd release up to a dozen singles and then summarize them with two albums a year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Canada's Early Embrace (1963-1964)
xref.body: The Beatles were embraced in Canada nearly a year before their breakthrough in the United States, with songs like "All My Love," "Roll Over Bay, Tovon," and "Twist and Shout" exclusively available there. Capitol Records Canada played a crucial role by manufacturing these records north of the 49th parallel and then exporting at least 100,000, and potentially up to 350,000, copies of each song to the US. "Although the United States gets a lot of attention because it's where the Beatles made their TV debut, it was in Canada where they were embraced first."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Christmas Flexi-Discs (1963-1969)
xref.body: The Beatles were notable for their extensive use of flexi-discs, sending out special Christmas flexi-discs to their fan club every year between 1963 and 1969. "The Beatles loved these things. Between 1963 and 1969, they sent out special Christmas flexis to the fan club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Co-owner of Northern Songs (February 1963)
xref.body: John Lennon was one of the initial owners of Northern Songs, the company that handled The Beatles' publishing starting in February 1963. "The owners were Dick James, Manager Brian Epstein, John Lennon, and Paul McCarty."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Disastrous Merchandising Deal (1963)
xref.body: In 1963, Beatles manager Brian Epstein licensed the band's merchandising rights to Nikki Bern's company, Selltab (Beatles spelled backwards). This deal secured only 10% of revenues for The Beatles and is estimated to have cost the band over $100 million over the years, despite selling a wide array of items from wigs to bubblegum. "In retrospect, this was a stupid deal, securing just 10% in revenues for the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Canadian Disinterest (1963)
xref.body: Despite their eventual global success, The Beatles initially struggled to gain traction in Canada in early 1963. Capitol Records Canada reported very low sales for their early singles: "Love Me Do" sold 170 copies, "Please Please Me" sold 280, and "From Me to You" sold 300, suggesting Canada was initially uninterested. "It seemed that Canada was not interested in the Beatles, but that all changed with the release of She Loves You in September 1963."

xref.title: 1964 Cultural Impact
xref.body: Starting in 1964, The Beatles' arrival marked a period in the 1960s where every day brought something new, exciting, and groundbreaking to music, profoundly shaping the decade's history. "starting with the Beatles in 1964 every day seemed to bring something new, something exciting and something groundbreaking."

xref.title: 1964 North American Tour & Ed Sullivan Appearance
xref.body: By the spring of 1964, The Beatles had achieved massive popularity not only in their home country but also across North America. This included performances in New York, Washington, and Miami in February, alongside their famous appearance on the Ed Sullivan Show, all generating immense buzz. "In February, the group had played New York, Washington and Miami, had appeared on the Ed Sullivan show, and they were attracting the same sort of buzz they had at home."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Brief Montreal Stay (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles played two concerts at the Montreal Forum on September 8, 1964, performing a 12-song set for 9,500 fans at 5:20 pm and another show for 11,500 fans at 8:30 pm. They chose not to stay in Montreal, instead flying directly to Jacksonville, Florida, having been in the city for only eight hours. "The band stayed in Montreal for only 8 hours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Brief Vancouver Performance (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' concert in Vancouver on August 22, 1964, despite the massive anticipation and crowd frenzy, lasted only 27 minutes. They played 11 songs, notably omitting "I Want to Hold Your Hand," one of their biggest hits at the time. Immediately after the show, the band was whisked away to Vancouver International Airport and flown straight to Los Angeles, marking their one and only performance in Western Canada. "Then just 27 minutes after they arrived on stage, they left."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bryce Decker's Airport Escapade (1964)
xref.body: On August 18, 1964, local high school student Bryce Decker took a daring chance at Winnipeg airport during The Beatles' refueling stop. He ran across the runway, climbed the plane's stairs, and nearly entered the aircraft before being restrained by security, an escapade that was captured in a series of photographs. Decker later recalled seeing the band members chuckling as security wrestled with him, having "just did it for a bit of fun" without realizing its significance. "After arriving at the airport, he ran across the runway, up the stairs, and nearly got into the plane before he was grouted by security."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Chaotic Toronto Airport Arrival (1964)
xref.body: On September 6, 1964, over 10,000 young people stormed Toronto's international airport to catch their first glimpse of The Beatles. The frenzied crowd jostled behind a 60-meter chain-link fence, belting out verses from their chart-topping tracks and screaming in a way the city had never heard before. "Behind a 60 meter chain link fence, the frenzy crowd jostled for position and belted out verses from chart crushing tracks such as, Please, please me, love, be, do, and she loves you."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Concert Logistics at Maple Leaf Gardens (1964)
xref.body: For the September 6, 1964, concerts at Maple Leaf Gardens, a detailed plan was devised to get The Beatles safely to the venue. Limousines served as a decoy, drawing fans while the band slipped out the back door of the King Edward Hotel and into a paddy wagon, which smuggled them into the Gardens. A five-block area around the venue was sectioned off 12 hours prior, transforming downtown Toronto into "Beedleland." "Limos were to pull up at the King Edward Hotel, as expected, as fans pounded at the vehicles like zombies the band would dug out the back door and into a patty wagon that would smuggle them into the gardens."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cultural Storm Example (1964-1970)
xref.body: The Beatles are cited as a prime example of a "perfect cultural storm" in music, where musical, social, political, and demographic conditions converged, with their most impactful era spanning from 1964 to 1970. "Think of the Beatles from 64 to 70."
