srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ed Sullivan Performance - John Cummings' Inspiration (1964)
xref.body: John Cummings (later Johnny Ramone) was deeply influenced by seeing The Beatles perform on The Ed Sullivan Show in 1964, sparking his love for the guitar. "He had been in love with the guitar ever since he saw the Beatles' plan Ed Sullivan back in 1964."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' debut performance on The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, is considered a watershed moment that irrevocably changed rock and roll forever. This pivotal event, which profoundly reshaped music history, might not have happened had Sullivan's flight not been delayed and if The Beatles had not coincidentally been at Heathrow Airport at the same time.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

xref.title: First North American Tour Stop in Winnipeg (1964)
xref.body: On a warm, cloudy day in mid-August 1964, The Beatles were flying from London to San Francisco for their inaugural major North American tour, making an unplanned refueling stop in Winnipeg. This stop unexpectedly turned into a major event when CJAYTV's Bob Burns announced their arrival on local radio, leading to the airport being swarmed by frenzied fans. "The band landed on August 18, 1964 at 2.5pm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Official Canadian Performance in Vancouver (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' first official Canadian concert and performance took place on August 22, 1964, at the Pacific National Exhibition (PNE) in Vancouver, British Columbia. The PNE is an annual 15-day summer fair and amusement park. "And the concert was held at the Pacific National Exhibition in Vancouver, British Columbia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hotel Invasion by Fans (1964)
xref.body: During The Beatles' stay at the King Edward Hotel in Toronto in September 1964, teens relentlessly bypassed security, creating an "infestation" for which the hotel seemed to have "no repellent." At 3 am, radio journalist Larry Cain, traveling with the band, encountered a teen in an oversized housekeeping uniform knocking on his door, asking for soap and then if he could take her to The Beatles. "Teens kept getting past security. It was as if the hotel was dealing with an infestation for which they had no repellent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

xref.title: Identical Second Toronto Concert (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' second concert at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto, which began at 10 pm on September 6, 1964, was virtually identical to the first. It featured screaming fans, blinding flash bulbs, raining lipsticks and bras, resulting in continued frenzy and fainting among the audience, echoing the "mass hysteria" of the earlier show. "If you've seen footage from a Beatles concert, you can imagine that the second concert was identical to the first."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impact of Ed Sullivan Show Debut (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' debut performance on The Ed Sullivan Show on February 9, 1964, is considered a watershed moment that irrevocably changed rock and roll forever. This pivotal event, which profoundly reshaped music history, might not have happened had Sullivan's flight not been delayed and if The Beatles had not coincidentally been at Heathrow Airport at the same time.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impact on Guitar Band Demand (1964)
xref.body: Following The Beatles' arrival in America in February 1964, there was an unprecedented surge in demand for electric guitars, as countless aspiring musicians were inspired to form guitar bands. This event marked a significant turning point in the popularity of the electric guitar. "After the Beatles hit America in February 1964, everyone wanted to be in a guitar band. Demand for new instruments exploded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

xref.title: John Lennon's Clash with Red Robinson (1964)
xref.body: Halfway through the Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, as the crowd neared rioting, local radio host Red Robinson was instructed to go on stage to calm the fans. John Lennon, unaware of the situation, confronted Robinson, telling him, "Get off our stage, nobody interrupts the Beatles," before relenting after Robinson explained that manager Brian Epstein had sent him. "John looked down at Brian Epstein, the band's manager who gave him the okay. John turned Robinson and said, Okay, carry on mate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: King Edward Hotel Frenzy (1964)
xref.body: Upon their arrival at the King Edward Hotel in downtown Toronto on September 6, 1964, a frenzy of fans greeted The Beatles, leading to Paul McCartney having his shirt torn and Ringo Starr being separated from John and George. Although police quickly restored order on the street, Beatlemania continued inside, where a 14-year-old girl was found hiding in the linen closet of their royal suite. "Paul would have a shirt torn open by a fan, wrangle with separated from John and George, but thankfully police were able to quickly restore order on the street and get the band into the hotel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mass Hysteria at Maple Leaf Gardens (1964)
xref.body: Upon The Beatles' appearance on stage at Maple Leaf Gardens on September 6, 1964, flash bulbs went off, blinding everyone, and the roar of 16,761 screaming voices made it impossible to hear the music, blinding and deafening the band. Items like bras and lipsticks rained down, leading to 109 fans fainting at the venue, described as "mass hysteria" rather than just a rock show. "It's unclear if they could even hear their own voices over the roar of 16,761 streaming voices, nor do we know if they could see anything as bras, lipsticks, and other items rain down on them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Massive Police Deployment in Toronto (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' first visit to Toronto in September 1964 necessitated an extraordinary police response, with more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario Provincial Police, and the counties called in. By noon, 4,000 police officers and auxiliaries were on duty around Maple Leaf Gardens, dividing the crowd into smaller sections, with majestic horses used to push back waves of "deranged youth." "The band's first visit to Toronto required more than 850 officers from the city, the Ontario provincial police, and the counties."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mayor Phil Givens Snubbed (1964)
xref.body: On September 6, 1964, Toronto mayor Phil Givens and his wife attempted to visit The Beatles at the King Edward Hotel at 1:30 pm but were turned away by a "blonde woman." She claimed two of the Beatles were sleeping and two were with relatives, an incident that led to the Daily Star publishing an article with the headline, "Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor." "The next day, the daily star released an article with the headline, Beatles Blonde, Snob is Mayor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Montreal Arrival and Death Threats (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' arrival at Dorval Airport for their only visit to La Belle province mirrored the scenes at other tour stops, with hordes of screaming fans. However, their time in Quebec was significantly marred by death threats from French Canadian separatists, specifically the FLQ, leading to the presence of police sharpshooters at the Montreal Forum on St. Catherine Street for their two concerts. "Their arrival at the Dorval Airport mirrored what happened at every stop on their tour. Hordes of screaming fans at the airport throngs of fans lying the streets, clutching magazines and singing their favorite Beatles songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening Act for The Beatles (1964)
xref.body: Bill Black's Combo served as an opening act for The Beatles' concert at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto on September 6, 1964. However, like the other supporting acts, they were met with boos from the impatient crowd, who were exclusively eager to see The Beatles perform. "As the opening bands, which included Bill Black's combo...hit the stage to crowd-bood, they only wanted one band, and one band only."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening Act for The Beatles (1964)
xref.body: The Exciters performed as one of the opening bands for The Beatles at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto on September 6, 1964. They, along with the other supporting acts, were booed by the crowd, whose sole focus was on seeing The Beatles. "As the opening bands, which included...the exciders...hit the stage to crowd-bood, they only wanted one band, and one band only."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening Act for The Beatles (1964)
xref.body: Clarence "Frogman" Henry was an opening act for The Beatles at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto on September 6, 1964. His performance, like those of the other support acts, was met with boos from an audience solely interested in the main event. "As the opening bands, which included...Clarence Frogman Henry...hit the stage to crowd-bood, they only wanted one band, and one band only."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening Act for The Beatles (1964)
xref.body: Jackie De Shannon was one of the opening acts for The Beatles' concert at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto on September 6, 1964. She, along with the other support acts, was booed by the audience who were impatient and only wanted to see The Beatles. "As the opening bands, which included...the Celterie Jackie De Shannon hit the stage to crowd-bood, they only wanted one band, and one band only."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening Acts Booed by Impatient Crowd (1964)
xref.body: At the Maple Leaf Gardens concert in Toronto on September 6, 1964, the opening bands, which included Bill Black's Combo, The Exciters, Clarence "Frogman" Henry, and Jackie De Shannon, were met with boos from the crowd. The audience was impatient and made it clear they wanted only one band: The Beatles. "As the opening bands, which included Bill Black's combo, the exciders Clarence Frogman Henry, and the Celterie Jackie De Shannon hit the stage to crowd-bood, they only wanted one band, and one band only."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pan Am Flight 101 Arrival - February 7, 1964
xref.body: The band's arrival on Pan Am Flight 101 from London at JFK Airport in New York on February 7, 1964, symbolized a massive explosion of Britishness and national pride. This event was referenced as a benchmark for the level of national pride seen again during the Britpop era. "an explosion of pride in Britishness that we really hadn't seen since February 7, 1964 when Pan Am Flight 101 from London touched down at JFK Airport in New York carrying a band called The Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

xref.title: Peaceful Departure from Toronto (1964)
xref.body: The day after their chaotic concerts, just before noon on September 7, 1964, The Beatles headed back to the Toronto airport. The sun was shining, the crowd was considerably smaller than the previous day, and the mood was distinctly different. The band signed autographs, posed for photos, waved to their admirers, and then boarded their plane, marking the end of their first Toronto visit. "The sun was shining, and the crowd was considerably smaller. The mood was also different. This was the end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Concert Activities and Press Conference (1964)
xref.body: After their first concert at Maple Leaf Gardens ended around 6 pm on September 6, 1964, The Beatles were quickly moved to a dressing room. There, they took photographs with local DJs, fan club presidents, and Miss Canada, followed by a press conference where they appeared somewhat bewildered but maintained their charming demeanor and "savage wit" towards journalists. "They then had a press conference where they looked a little bewildered, but as usual they were charming to admirers, and unleashed their savage wit on journalists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ringo Starr's Worry Over Montreal Threats (1964)
xref.body: Ringo Starr expressed genuine worry about the death threats received during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal concerts. He recalled that some individuals targeted him "as an English Jew," despite him not being Jewish, noting that while threats were often taken "in stride," this particular incident, despite more police presence, was one of the few times he was truly concerned. "Some people decided to make an example of me as an English Jew. The one major fault is, I'm not Jewish. Threats we took in stride. I mean, suddenly there'd be a few more cops, but this was one of the few times I was really worried."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rock's Rescuers (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles are credited with rescuing rock music after a period of decline, creating a widespread "tsunami" that influenced music for the remainder of the 1960s. "The Beatles, of course, rescued Rock, created this tsunami that spread across the planet, and it lasted the rest of the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

xref.title: Vancouver Concert Delay and Paperwork (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, was scheduled for 8 pm, but a significant delay occurred because the pilot of their plane forgot to sign a required document. This forced the band to return to the airport to complete the paperwork, while 20,000 fans impatiently waited at the stadium. "The show was supposed to start at 8pm, but the pilot of the plane bringing the Beatles to Canada forgot to sign a document, and the band was forced to return to the airport to finish the paperwork and then head back to the stadium."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Creative Output in 1965
xref.body: The Beatles were highly active and influential in 1965, contributing significantly to a prolific year for rock music and its role as an agent for social change. "the Beatles and everything they were doing"

xref.title: Return to Toronto and Fading Beatlemania (1965)
xref.body: On August 17, 1965, The Beatles returned to Canada, flying in from New York to Pearson Airport (then Toronto International Airport), where fans again rushed them, met by Toronto police. They stayed at the King Edward Hotel, where "smart fans" booked dozens of rooms. However, the enthusiasm had waned slightly, as newspaper coverage shifted from front-page headlines to inside pages, with many suggesting that Beatlemania was fading and the band's popularity might soon disappear. "Unlike the previous year when the band made front page news in Toronto, this year, they were on the inside pages, with many starting to say that Biddlemania was fading, and the band would soon disappear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shea Stadium Sound Disaster (1965)
xref.body: When The Beatles played Shea Stadium on August 15, 1965, there was no proper concert sound system for the venue. They set up on a small stage, using a bunch of mics and a couple of 100 Watt Vox amplifiers, and pumped everything through the stadium's public address system—the same speakers and amplifiers used for baseball announcements. It was so bad that the Beatles not only couldn't be heard by the audience but also couldn't hear themselves. "As a last second fix, one of the road crew flipped over some of their amplifiers and pointed them directly at the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shift Towards Album as Artistic Statement (Circa 1965)
xref.body: Around 1965, prominent artists such as The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and The Beach Boys began to pivot from focusing on individual singles towards conceptualizing albums as complete artistic statements, typically comprising ten, twelve, or more interconnected tracks. "But starting in around 1965, a number of artists, the Beatles, Bob Dylan, and the Beach Boys among them, began to think less in terms of individual songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shifting Album Perception (c. 1965)
xref.body: Around 1965, The Beatles, alongside Bob Dylan and others, began to view the album as a medium for artistic expression, leading them to write longer, more complex, and carefully sequenced collections of songs rather than just single-focused releases. "The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and a few others looked at the album and thought, I can work with this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shifting Album Perception (c. 1965)
xref.body: Around 1965, Bob Dylan, along with The Beatles, recognized the album's potential as a cohesive artistic work, which prompted a shift towards writing longer, more complex songs and sequenced collections rather than simply releasing singles. "The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and a few others looked at the album and thought, I can work with this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "More Popular Than Jesus" Comment (1966)
xref.body: In 1966, John Lennon made a controversial remark claiming that The Beatles were "more popular than Jesus." This comment was considered blasphemous by broadcasters Tommy Charles and Doug Layton in Birmingham, Alabama, who subsequently launched a campaign to ban The Beatles, resulting in public record destruction. "And when John Lennon made a flippin' comment in 1966 about the Beatles being more popular than Jesus, two broadcasters, Tommy Charles and Doug Layton from Birmingham, Alabama, started a campaign to ban the Beatles over this blasphemy, and many records were broken and burned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Departure from Canada (1966)
xref.body: After their final concerts in Toronto on August 17, 1966, The Beatles stayed overnight before flying out to Boston on August 18th. This departure marked their definitive farewell to Canadian stages, as they never toured again. "This time, they left forever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early End to Touring (1966)
xref.body: Following the terrible sound experience at Shea Stadium in 1965, where they were miserable due to not being able to hear themselves, The Beatles played their last proper live gig a year later. The severe issues with concert sound reinforcement directly contributed to their decision to never tour again. "A year later, they played their last proper live gig, and they never toured again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Final Toronto Concerts (1966)
xref.body: On August 17, 1966, The Beatles performed their last Canadian concerts in Toronto, with 15,000 fans attending the first show and 17,000 for the second at 8 pm. Bill J. Nelson served as MC, and the routine chaos continued, with 50 audience members treated for shock and screaming volumes making the music barely audible. "That number only went up to 17,000 fans for their second concert at 8pm."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Last Canadian and Touring Concerts (1966)
xref.body: The Beatles returned to Canada on August 17, 1966, for their final two concerts ever on Canadian soil in Toronto. This tour also marked the last time the band would ever play live, consisting of only eight shows over 12 days before they stopped touring forever to focus exclusively on studio music. "Just a year later in 1966, the band returned for their last two concerts ever on Canadian soil. The tour was also the last the band would ever play."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-1966 Studio Band Fades
xref.body: After 1966, when The Beatles stopped touring and evolved into a studio band, they frequently incorporated fade-outs into their songs. This allowed them to avoid crafting a definitive ending for a live audience, opting instead for an artistic or technical fade. "The Beatles were big into the fade after 1966 when they stopped touring and became a studio band and no longer had to properly finish a song for a live audience."

xref.body: After Brian Epstein's death in 1967, The Beatles' business affairs became chaotic. Relations with Dick James soured, leading him to sell his share of Northern Songs to ATV Music without informing John Lennon and Paul McCartney, who were upset and attempted unsuccessfully to buy James's share themselves. "After Manager Brian Epstein died in 1967, the business affairs of the Beatles were in shambles. Relations between the group and Dick James music soured, and Dick James wanted out of Northern Songs. That's when he sold his share to a company called ATV Music without giving any notice to John and Paul."

xref.title: Formation and Members (1967)
xref.body: The band was formed in 1967 by James Newell Osterberg (Iggy), brothers Ron and Scott Ashton, and Dave Alexander. Iggy, who was a known drummer in Ann Arbor, befriended Ron Ashton, leading to Scott joining, and then Dave Alexander, a high school dropout who had traveled the UK in search of the meaning of The Beatles. "These four guys decided to form a band with Iggy out front and on keyboards."

xref.title: The Residents (Shreveport LA, 1969) – No Known Members; Hardy W. Fox Died 2018 Listed as Co-Founder; George Harrison and Claypool Denied
xref.body: The Residents are an art collective that originated in Shreveport, Louisiana in 1969. By 1971 they were performing in San Francisco. They have never shown their faces or listed any band members — their only point of contact is a company called Cryptic Music. When their debut album Meet the Residents was released in 1974 (parodying the Beatles' Meet the Beatles), some fans believed they were actually the Beatles in disguise. Hardy W. Fox — who claimed to have been a Resident — died in 2018 with his obituary listing him as co-founder and primary songwriter. Other names tied to the band include Homer Cook (unconfirmed), Jay Clem (maybe), and "Charles Boebuck" (apparently a pseudonym for Fox). Contrary to rumors, George Harrison, Les Claypool of Primus, and no member of Devo has ever been in the band. "I can tell you, though, contrary to rumors, George Harrison less clay pool of primus, and no one from Devo has ever been in the residence."

xref.title: Toronto Rock and Roll Revival Performance (September 13, 1969)
xref.body: John Lennon performed at Varsity Stadium in Toronto, facing severe stage fright and heroin withdrawal, as it was his first performance outside The Beatles. He was also intimidated by other acts on the bill, including his idols Chuck Berry, Gene Vincent, and Little Richard. "This was the first time John had ever performed outside the Beatles, which at the time were still a going concern."

xref.title: 1970 Breakup and Lasting Influence
xref.body: The Beatles broke up in 1970, yet they are still considered the greatest and most influential rock group of all time, maintaining their status indefinitely. "Even though they broke up in 1970, they are still the greatest and most influential rock group of all time and will probably be forever."

xref.title: Name Change to Abbey Road (1970)
xref.body: The studio changed its name from EMI Studios to Abbey Road Studios in 1970. This change was prompted by the immense publicity generated by its most famous clients, The Beatles, who had released their album *Abbey Road* the previous year. "It stayed with the name EMI Studios until 1970, when the Beatles, their most famous clients, released an album called Abbey Road."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Beatles Sell Their Share to ATV Music (By January 1970)
xref.body: Following a dispute with ATV over their publishing share, and after their manager Allen Klein failed to secure the desired deal, The Beatles sold their remaining stake in Northern Songs to ATV Music. By January 1970, ATV owned 99% of The Beatles' publishing. This financial tension significantly contributed to the band's breakup a few months later. "Very, very long story short, they did not get the deal they wanted, so the Beatles sold their piece of Northern Songs to ATV. By January 1970, ATV owned 99% of the Beatles' publishing. This financial tension went a long ways towards the Beatles breaking up a few months later."

xref.title: Acquisition of Norvat Jack Music (1973)
xref.body: Following the loss of The Beatles' publishing, McCartney began acquiring other artists' catalogs in 1973, starting with Norvat Jack Music, which held many songs by his idol, Buddy Holly. This established a significant income stream for him. "He started in 1973 buying a company called Norvat Jack Music, which contained many of the songs by Buddy Holly, one of McCartney's idols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Beatles Collaboration with McCartney (1973)
xref.body: George Martin, who built and ran Air Studios in London, agreed to produce the recording sessions for Paul McCartney's "Live and Let Die" theme. This marked a significant reunion, as it was the first time Martin had worked with a Beatle since the conclusion of the "Abbey Road" sessions in 1969. Martin later compelled the Bond producers to use McCartney's version as the title sequence. "Martin agreed to produce the sessions marking this as the first time since the end of the Abbey Road sessions that he got to work with a beetle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Signing with EMI (1976) - Subversive Victory
xref.body: On October 8, 1976, the Sex Pistols signed a deal with EMI records for £40,000, which was considered a fortune at the time. This move was admired by the punk community, who saw it not as selling out, but as a "major subversive victory" for managing to "swindle such a huge amount of money from a gullible multinational major record label." "And the home of the Beatles no less. This was considered to be a major subversive victory for the punk rock cause."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: EMI Contract Termination (1977) - "Toxic" Band
xref.body: Following their infamous TV appearance and alleged public vomiting episodes, including one at Heathrow Airport (exaggerated by tabloids), the Sex Pistols became "toxic." EMI Records, the label of The Beatles and owner of Abbey Road studios, could no longer tolerate the controversy and paid the band £40,000 to terminate their contract. "So they paid the pistols 40,000 pounds to just go away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Glenn Matlock's Departure (February 1977)
xref.body: Matlock's departure was officially reported as a firing in February 1977 because he "liked The Beatles too much," specifically Paul McCartney, and allegedly washed his feet too often. This narrative was fabricated and fed to the press by manager Malcolm McLaren. In truth, Matlock quit due to intense friction with Johnny Rotten, McLaren's manipulative "head games," constant media attacks, canceled gigs, venue bans, lack of pay, and the physical assaults suffered by Johnny and Paul. "Glenn Matlock was fired in February 1977... Matlock wasn't fired. He quit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influential After 1977
xref.body: Kraftwerk is considered by some to be the most influential band in the world next to The Beatles, with their impact traceable in music starting anytime after 1977. Their influence spans EDM, techno (including Detroit techno and Daft Punk), ambient and chillout music, synth and sample-constructed music (like Simple Minds and Depeche Mode), early 80s techno pop (OMD, Soft Cell), and industrial music (Nine Inch Nails). "Pick any starting point in music anytime after 1977. And you will somehow be led back in some fashion to Craftwork."

xref.title: Sid Vicious' Recruitment (1977)
xref.body: In the spring of 1977, Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren insisted on Sid Vicious joining the band as a replacement for original bassist Glenn Matlock, who was allegedly fired for liking The Beatles too much. McLaren's decision was not based on Vicious's musical ability—he "couldn't name the strings on a bass, let alone play them"—but on the idea that it would be "cool if a fan was invited to join the group."

xref.title: Virgin Records Contract Signing (1977)
xref.body: Richard Branson of Virgin Records saw an opportunity after major labels rejected the Sex Pistols and signed them in 1977. This "smart move" led to the explosion of the Pistols and punk rock, significantly benefiting Virgin Records. "Branson though saw an opportunity and signed them up. Smart move."

xref.title: Hamilton Punk Provocateurs – "Surfin' on Heroin," Nazi Allegations, Cassette "Burn the Flag" (1978)
xref.body: The Forgotten Rebels formed in Hamilton in 1977, about 18 months after Teenage Head. Led by Mickey DeSadist, they were sarcastic, sometimes profane, and featured songs like "Surfin' on Heroin," "Bomb the Boats and Feed the Fish" (about Vietnamese refugees), "No Beatles Reunion," and a song called "Reich 'n' Roll" that drew allegations of anti-Semitism and homophobia; the band maintained it was all satire. Their first release was a six-song cassette called *Burn the Flag* in 1978, followed by *Tomorrow Belongs to Us*. They occasionally attracted crowds of several thousand. "They had a large cult following, although they were never really embraced to the level of Teenage Head."

xref.title: "Her Majesty" - Accidental Hidden Track
xref.body: The inclusion of "Her Majesty" as a hidden track on "Abbey Road" was an unintended consequence of studio procedure. After Paul McCartney requested the song's removal, tape assistant John Kerlander snipped it out and spliced it to the end of the master tape with 20 seconds of blank tape, in accordance with Abbey Road's rules for edited material. A mastering engineer either overlooked or misread Kerlander's note, resulting in the song's presence on the final master, which the Beatles found "really cool" and decided to keep. "And so the first hidden track came to be as the result of an accident."

xref.body: The Beatles were recognized as a major influence on young German musicians, alongside other British and American acts, but German artists ultimately sought to create something different rather than merely imitating them. This band is also cited as arguably the second most influential band in history after Kraftwerk. "It wasn't good enough just to imitate the Beatles of the Stones, something else, something different was required."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: The Stones were a significant musical hero for young Germans, but the new wave of German musicians aimed to move beyond mere imitation to forge a unique German sound. "It wasn't good enough just to imitate the Beatles of the Stones, something else, something different was required."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Assassination in New York City
xref.body: John Lennon, the most famous member of The Beatles, was murdered on Monday, December 8, 1980, outside his apartment building on the west side of New York City. He was shot twice in the back and rushed to Roosevelt Hospital, where he was pronounced dead on arrival. "John Lennon, outside of his apartment building on the west side of New York City. The most famous, perhaps, of all of the Beatles. Shot twice in the back, rushed to Roosevelt Hospital dead on arrival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Asteroid 8749 Beatles
xref.body: In 1998, an asteroid measuring between four and nine kilometers in diameter was discovered by astronomers at the Redie Creek Observatory in Australia. It was officially named 8749 Beatles and resides beyond the orbit of Mars. "It was given the name 8-7-49 Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: BBC Archive Recordings (Multiple Years)
xref.body: The Beatles are among the thousands of artists who were invited to make records at the BBC to circumvent "Needle Time" restrictions, which limited the amount of commercially available recorded music the BBC could play. These sessions contributed to the BBC's amazing archive of recordings. "Even from the Beatles to Bob Barley to Joy Division to Tears for Fiers and literally thousands of other artists were invited to make records at the BBC so they could get around the whole Needle Time thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Backmasking Pioneers
xref.body: The Beatles were extensively involved in backmasking, intentionally placing backward segments in their recordings, including songs like "Tomorrow Never Knows," "Rain," and throughout "The White Album." "The Beatles were very big into back masking. They experimented with backward bits and songs like Tomorrow and Ever-Knowes, Rain, and Throw Out the White Album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Lifespan Template Adherence
xref.body: The Clash is cited as a band that closely followed Don Letts' theory on the average useful lifespan of a band, which typically involves a period of intense activity, a peak around year four or five, and then an inevitable decline due to internal and external conflicts. "Now the clash certainly followed that template, sort of the Beatles and the Smiths."

xref.title: Band Lifespan and Best Work
xref.body: Don Letz, a DJ, filmmaker, and confidant of The Clash, noted that the average lifespan of a band is seven years, usually enough time for them to achieve success and then face internal conflicts. The Beatles' period of their most significant work was from 1963 to 1970, aligning with this seven-year pattern. "the Beatles from 63 to 70."

xref.title: Beatles Speculation (1970s)
xref.body: In the 1970s, there was widespread speculation that one version of The Residents was actually John, Paul, Ringo, and George in disguise, a rumor that was not true. "At one point in the 1970s, there was speculation that one version of the residence was actually John Paul Ringo and George in disguise. To be try, but not true."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Beatles-esque Sound
xref.body: Oasis is highlighted as a prime example of an artist whose sound is heavily based on the "vibe" of The Beatles, showcasing how admiration and respect for forebears can lead to creating material "in the same vein" with a modern twist. "A great example is Oasis. So much of their sound is based on the vibe we get from the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Biggest Impact on Rock and Roll Drums
xref.body: Ringo Starr is credited with having the biggest single impact on drumming in rock and roll history. When The Beatles burst into the mainstream in 1964, Ringo's distinctive persona, described as "fun and slightly odd-looking," drew many young people to the drums, making playing look enjoyable and accessible. "The biggest thing that ever happened to drums in rock and roll was Ringo Star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Billboard Top Five Record
xref.body: Elvis was one of only three rock acts in history to have two singles in the Billboard Top Five at the same time, a feat he achieved prior to Twenty One Pilots accomplishing it in 2016. "In 2016, they became just the third rock act in history to have two singles in the billboard top five at the same time, only Elvis and the Beatles had managed that."

xref.title: Breakup and Impact
xref.body: The band had broken up by the early 1970s, contributing to a sense that rock music, which had been a big part of sweeping social changes in the 1960s, was tired. Their breakup is cited alongside the deaths of other rock icons as a factor in the somber mood of the era. "The Beatles had broken up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: British Invasion Influence
xref.body: The Kinks are cited as one of the British Invasion bands that followed The Beatles, further developing the sound that would lead to Powerpop. They are considered an influence by later Powerpop acts like Big Star. "Through the Beatles came all the rest of the British invasion bands, especially the Kinks and the Who."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: British Invasion Influence
xref.body: The Who are recognized as one of the British Invasion bands that emerged after The Beatles, contributing to the evolving rock sound that formed the basis of Powerpop. Their guitarist, Pete Townsend, is specifically credited with coining the term "Powerpop." "Through the Beatles came all the rest of the British invasion bands, especially the Kinks and the Who."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: British Invasion Leader - 1960s
xref.body: The Beatles led the British Invasion in the 1960s, a movement that exemplified the British music scene's ability to create influential movements that stick. They were a key part of an explosion of British pride. "In the 1960s, it was the British invasion led by the Beatles and the Stones."

xref.title: British Rock Tradition
xref.body: Led Zeppelin was mentioned as part of the proud tradition of British rock and roll that needed to be saved from the "grunge marauders" invading from the US. "Her majesty's empire needed to be saved from the grunge marauders, the proud tradition of British rock and roll, the Beatles, the Stones, Led Zeppelin, Sexbistles, Clash, Bowie, it all needed to be saved from the likes of Nirvana and Pearl Jam and Soundgarden."
